Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⇒ & v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 4x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =4x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}-4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1-0\cdot 0)+4(0-1) \\  & =2\pi -4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0902a00b-6972-5278-913c-8072ffb99155"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0902a00b-6972-5278-913c-8072ffb99155" :answer-field/id #uuid "0902a00b-6972-5278-913c-8072ffb99155" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-81ae3e78-b1f4-5477-8bac-c412eb3c2747" :answer-field/choices ["answer-81ae3e78-b1f4-5477-8bac-c412eb3c2747"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-81ae3e78-b1f4-5477-8bac-c412eb3c2747" :answer/id #uuid "81ae3e78-b1f4-5477-8bac-c412eb3c2747" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065444 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we introduce a method of integration that can be used in cases where integration by substitution fails. The method is known as **integration by parts**. The so-called **by-parts formula** is 

$$
\int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x
$$

or simply

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

This method is handy for integrating products of functions where one factor can be easily integrated, and the other factor can easily be differentiated. 

Let's see how to apply it to evaluate the integral 

$$
\int xe^{2x} \textrm{d}x\,.
$$

The idea is to call one of the factors $u,$ the other factor $v',$ and then apply the by-parts formula. We'll choose the following:

$$
\int \underbrace{\color{blue}x}_{\large\color{blue}u}\cdot \underbrace{\color{red}e^{2x}}_{\large\color{red}v'} \textrm{d}x
$$

Now, if ${\color{blue}u} = {\color{blue}x}$ then we differentiate to get ${\color{blue}u'} = {\color{blue}1}.$ And if ${\color{red}v'} = {\color{red}e^{2x}}$ then we integrate to get ${\color{red}v} = {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}}.$ Note that we don't bother with the constant of integration here.

We now have everything we need, so we can substitute into the "by-parts" formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {{x\cdot {e}^{2x}}_{⏟}}_{u{v}^{′}}\,\text{d}x & ={{x\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}}_{⏟}}_{uv}-\int {{\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}\cdot 1}_{⏟}}_{v{u}^{′}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}(2x-1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done! Notice that integration by parts allows us to take a complicated integral $\displaystyle \int xe^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x$ and replace it with the simpler $\displaystyle \int e^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x$ plus some additional terms." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065446 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our first example,

$$
\int xe^{2x} \textrm{d}x\,.
$$

Note that when we selected our $u$ and $v',$ we could have picked them the other way around. So instead, we could have said

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2{e}^{2x} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the by-parts formula using this selection, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{2x}-\int {x}^{2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, while the above is a mathematically correct statement, the integral on the right-hand side is *more* complicated than the integral we started with. Ouch!

Therefore, it's crucial that we select our $u$ and $v'$ in such a way that the problem is simplified, not made more complicated." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064413 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

substitution fails. The method is known as **integration by parts**. The so-called **by-parts formula** is \n\n$$\n\\int u\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}v}{\\textrm{d}x}\\,\\textrm{d}x= uv- \\int v\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}u}{\\textrm{d}x}\\,\\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nor simply\n\n$$\n\\int uv'\\,\\textrm{d}x= uv- \\int vu'\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis method is handy for integrating products of functions where one factor can be easily integrated, and the other factor can easily be differentiated. \n\nLet's see how to apply it to evaluate the integral \n\n$$\n\\int xe^{2x} \\textrm{d}x\\,.\n$$\n\nThe idea is to call one of the factors $u,$ the other factor $v',$ and then apply the by-parts formula. We'll choose the following:\n\n$$\n\\int \\underbrace{\\color{blue}x}_{\\large\\color{blue}u}\\cdot \\underbrace{\\color{red}e^{2x}}_{\\large\\color{red}v'} \\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nNow, if ${\\color{blue}u} = {\\color{blue}x}$ then we differentiate to get ${\\color{blue}u'} = {\\color{blue}1}.$ And if ${\\color{red}v'} = {\\color{red}e^{2x}}$ then we integrate to get ${\\color{red}v} = {\\color{red}\\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}}.$ Note that we don't bother with the constant of integration here.\n\nWe now have everything we need, so we can substitute into the \"by-parts\" formula, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {{x\\cdot {e}^{2x}}_{⏟}}_{u{v}^{'}}\\,\\text{d}x & ={{x\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}}_{⏟}}_{uv}-\\int {{\\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}\\cdot 1}_{⏟}}_{v{u}^{'}}\\,\\text{d}x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we compute the integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int x{e}^{2x}\\,\\text{d}x & =\\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{2x}-\\frac{1}{2}\\int {e}^{2x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{2x}-\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+C \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{2x}-\\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}+C \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}(2x-1)+C\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAnd we're done! Notice that integration by parts allows us to take a complicated integral $\\displaystyle \\int xe^{2x}\\,\\textrm{d}x$ and replace it with the simpler $\\displaystyle \\int e^{2x}\\,\\textrm{d}x$
